title: Harrigan
origin: Words and music by George M. Cohan, published 1907, from the musical Fifty Miles from Boston
note: Written as a tribute to Cohan's Irish-American heritage, its title spelled out letter by letter in the chorus. Public domain since 1907.
verses:
Who is the man who will spend or will even lend?
Who is the man who will treat all hands from town to town?
Who is the man they call on to save a stranded show?
Who is the man that ev'rybody ought to know?
It's Harrigan, that's me!

title: Mary's a Grand Old Name
origin: Words and music by George M. Cohan, published 1905, from the musical Forty-Five Minutes from Broadway
note: A cheerful courting song built around the simplicity and endurance of the name Mary. Public domain since 1905.
verses:
Did you ever notice that ev'rybody has a joke on Mary?
A fact quite true, I'm telling you, in a great big city, small town, or village,
Have you not heard folks say?
Up goes the price of veal and pork,
Up goes the price of coal and pork,
But Mary is a name that no one can spoil.

title: Peg O' My Heart
origin: Words by Alfred Bryan, music by Fred Fisher, published 1913, written for the Ziegfeld Follies
note: Written for a musical of the same name, this became one of the most enduring hits of the pre-WWI era. Public domain since 1913.
verses:
Dear face that makes my nights so lonely,
Sighing for the smile that's only,
Set like a star in the blue,
Dear little girl, so full of coquetry,
In her eyes-a look of mischief you'll see.

Peg o' my heart, I love you,
We'll never part, I love you,
Dear little girl of mine,
I always knew, it's true, sweet Peg,
Oh, it was you were sent from Heaven,
And I know your name is Peg.

title: Moonlight Bay
origin: Words by Edward Madden, music by Percy Wenrich, published 1912
note: A romantic barbershop-style waltz, later famously referenced in the 1953 film By the Light of the Silvery Moon. Public domain since 1912.
verses:
We were sailing along, on Moonlight Bay,
We could hear the voices ringing,
They seemed to say,
You have stolen my heart, now don't go 'way,
As we sang love's old sweet song, on Moonlight Bay.

title: I Want a Girl (Just Like the Girl That Married Dear Old Dad)
origin: Words by William Dillon, music by Harry Von Tilzer, published 1911
note: A sentimental tribute to the singer's mother, framed as an ideal for a future bride. One of the best-selling songs of 1911. Public domain since 1911.
verses:
I never see a pretty girl who's fat and forty-two,
I think perhaps she's someone's mother, so I says to you,
Boys, I'm certainly glad I met you, hope that you will meet my mother when you can.

I want a girl, just like the girl that married dear old dad,
She was a pearl, and the only girl that daddy ever had,
A good old fashioned girl with heart so true,
One who loves nothing but you,
I want a girl, just like the girl that married dear old dad.

title: Row, Row, Row
origin: Words by William Jerome, music by James V. Monaco, published 1912
note: A comic boating-and-courting song, not to be confused with the older children's round of a similar name. Public domain since 1912.
verses:
Ida, sweet as apple cider, sweeter than lemonader,
Come and take a trip with me, up the river,
Oh, so quiet, no one'll spy her,
With her honey boy, oh joy!

Row, row, row, up the river he would row, row, row,
A hug he'd give her, then he'd kiss her now and then,
She would tell him when, he would tell her not to be so slow,
That's why they all love to row.

title: The Twa Brothers
origin: Traditional Scottish/English ballad, Child Ballad No. 49, documented from the 18th century
note: A tragic ballad of an accidental fatal wound given in play between two brothers, one of the most widely collected Child ballads in American oral tradition. Ancient and public domain.
verses:
There were two brothers at the school,
And when they got awa',
'It's will ye play at the stane-chuckin',
Or will ye play at the ba',
Or will ye gae up to yon hill head,
And there we'll wrestle a fa'?'

'I winna play at the stane-chuckin',
Nor will I play at the ba',
But I'll gae up to yon bonnie green hill,
And there we'll wrestle a fa'.'

They wrestled up, they wrestled down,
Till John fell to the ground,
A dirk fell out of William's pouch,
And gave John a deadly wound.

title: Johnie Scot
origin: Traditional Scottish ballad, Child Ballad No. 99, documented from the 18th century
note: A ballad of a Scottish lord who champions his beloved through single combat against an English king's champion. Ancient and public domain.
verses:
Johnie Scot's a hunting gane,
Unto the woods sae wild,
And bonnie Jean, his lovesome May,
She's greatest wi' his child.

'If that I be wi' bairn,' she says,
'As I trust weel I be,
Ye'll carry me down to bonnie Scotland,
And there ye'll marry me.'

'Aft hae I brought to Paris toun,
The robes that ye do wear,
But I'll bring wi' me a better man,
Or I've been shamed here.'

title: The Fair Flower of Northumberland
origin: Traditional English/Scottish ballad, Child Ballad No. 9, documented in broadside form from the 16th-17th century
note: A border ballad of a young woman who helps a Scottish prisoner escape for love, only to be abandoned by him once safely across the border. Ancient and public domain.
verses:
It was a knight in Scotland born,
Follow, my love, come over the strand,
Was taken prisoner and left forlorn,
Even by the good Earl of Northumberland.

'Fair maid, if you will pity me,
And help me out of prison strong,
I'll marry you when I am free,
And take you into fair Scotland.'

She stole from her father's pillow the key,
And out of prison she set him free,
She took him to her father's stable,
And gave to him the best steed there.

title: Hind Etin
origin: Traditional Scottish ballad, Child Ballad No. 41, with roots in older Scandinavian ballad tradition, documented from the 18th century
note: A ballad in which a lady is carried off by a forest-dwelling outlaw and eventually finds happiness with him, in a rare Child ballad with a peaceful resolution. Ancient and public domain.
verses:
May Margaret sits in her bower door,
Sewing at her seam,
She heard a note in Elmond's wood,
And wished she there had been.

She loot the seam fa' frae her side,
And the needle to her tae,
And she is on to Elmond wood,
As fast as she could gae.

She hadna pu'd a nut, a nut,
A nut but barely three,
Till up and started a young Hind Etin,
Says, 'Let alane the tree.'

title: The Banks of Newfoundland
origin: Traditional capstan shanty, documented aboard emigrant and packet ships crossing the North Atlantic by the mid-19th century
note: A homeward-bound shanty referencing the treacherous Grand Banks fishing grounds off Newfoundland, a notorious hazard for sailing ships. Traditional and public domain.
verses:
Oh, the times are hard and the wages low,
Away, ho, boys, away, ho,
The Leviathan for New York must go,
We're bound for the Banks of Newfoundland.

And it's now we're bound for the Banks of Newfoundland,
Where the ocean's deep and the mountains high,
Where the sea and the whale come skimmin' by,
We're bound for the Banks of Newfoundland.

title: Rolling Home
origin: Traditional capstan shanty, documented aboard sailing ships trading between England and the New World by the mid-19th century
note: A joyous homeward-bound shanty, sung with anticipation of a safe return after a long ocean voyage. Traditional and public domain.
verses:
Call all hands to man the capstan,
See the cable run down clear,
Heave away, and with a will, boys,
For old England we will steer.

Rolling home, rolling home,
Rolling home across the sea,
Rolling home to dear old England,
Rolling home, dear land, to thee.

title: Whiskey Johnny
origin: Traditional halyard shanty, documented aboard sailing ships by the mid-19th century
note: A rousing hauling shanty celebrating (and lamenting) whiskey's hold over sailors ashore. Traditional and public domain.
verses:
Oh, whiskey is the life of man,
Whiskey, Johnny,
I'll drink whiskey while I can,
Whiskey for my Johnny.

Whiskey up and whiskey down,
Whiskey, Johnny,
Whiskey all around the town,
Whiskey for my Johnny.

Whiskey killed my poor old dad,
Whiskey, Johnny,
Whiskey drove my mother mad,
Whiskey for my Johnny.

title: O Come, All Ye Faithful (Adeste Fideles)
origin: Latin hymn text traditionally attributed to John Francis Wade, c. 1743; English translation by Frederick Oakeley, 1841
note: One of the most widely sung Christmas carols in the world, originally circulated in Latin among English Catholic communities before its 19th-century English translation. Public domain.
verses:
O come, all ye faithful,
Joyful and triumphant,
O come ye, O come ye to Bethlehem,
Come and behold Him,
Born the King of angels.

O come, let us adore Him,
O come, let us adore Him,
O come, let us adore Him,
Christ the Lord.

Sing, choirs of angels,
Sing in exultation,
Sing, all ye citizens of heaven above,
Glory to God,
Glory in the highest.

title: Once in Royal David's City
origin: Words by Cecil Frances Alexander, published 1848; music by Henry John Gauntlett, 1849
note: Written for children by an Irish hymn writer, this carol traditionally opens the Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols at King's College, Cambridge. Public domain since 1848.
verses:
Once in royal David's city,
Stood a lowly cattle shed,
Where a mother laid her baby,
In a manger for His bed,
Mary was that mother mild,
Jesus Christ her little child.

He came down to earth from heaven,
Who is God and Lord of all,
And His shelter was a stable,
And His cradle was a stall,
With the poor and mean and lowly,
Lived on earth our Saviour holy.

title: Sinner Man
origin: Traditional African American spiritual, documented in spiritual and gospel-blues collections of the early 20th century
note: A dramatic spiritual describing a sinner's futile search for refuge on judgment day, in the same tradition as 'There's No Hiding Place.' Traditional and public domain.
verses:
Oh, sinner man, where you gonna run to?
Oh, sinner man, where you gonna run to?
Oh, sinner man, where you gonna run to?
All on that day.

Run to the rock, rock won't you hide me?
Run to the rock, rock won't you hide me?
Run to the rock, rock won't you hide me?
All on that day.

Run to the sea, sea is a-boiling,
Run to the sea, sea is a-boiling,
Run to the sea, sea is a-boiling,
All on that day.
